metadata.name: lambda
metadata.overview:
AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code without requiring you to provision or manage servers. Lambda manages the underlying infrastructure, including server maintenance, capacity provisioning, automatic scaling, and patching. You supply code as a .zip archive or a container image, and Lambda runs it inside an isolated, service-managed execution environment.

Lambda is event driven. Other AWS services, HTTP endpoints, message queues, data streams, and direct API calls can all trigger your code. Lambda creates and destroys execution environments to match demand, and it applies security and functional updates to its managed language runtimes. For work that spans many steps, Lambda can checkpoint progress so an execution resumes after an interruption instead of restarting.

Access is governed through AWS Identity and Access Management. An execution role grants a function the permissions it needs to reach other AWS resources, while identity-based and resource-based policies control who and what may invoke it. Functions can attach to a virtual private cloud to reach private resources, stream logs and traces to monitoring and analytics destinations, and encrypt configuration values, code artifacts, and workflow state with managed or customer-controlled keys.
useCases: Event-driven file and object processing — invoking a function automatically when objects are created, deleted or modified in an Amazon S3 bucket (for example generating thumbnails or transforming uploaded data)
Serverless web/mobile/IoT API backends — fronting functions with Amazon API Gateway, an Application Load Balancer, or a Lambda function URL to serve HTTP(S) requests without managing servers

Real-time stream and queue processing — using event source mappings to consume batches of records from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon DynamoDB Streams, Amazon SQS, Amazon MSK/self-managed Apache Kafka, Amazon MQ, and Amazon DocumentDB change streams

Scheduled and periodic automation, security remediation, and operational tasks — invoked by EventBridge rules/EventBridge Scheduler or AWS Config, and used as custom Config rule evaluators, Security Hub custom actions, Secrets Manager rotation functions, and CloudFormation custom resources

Long-running, stateful multi-step workflows with Lambda Durable Functions — checkpointed executions that can run for up to one year for order processing, approval workflows, human-in-the-loop processes, and complex data pipelines

Multi-tenant SaaS platforms that execute end-user-supplied or AI-generated code, using tenant isolation mode (Firecracker-isolated per-tenant execution environments) or Lambda MicroVMs for stronger workload isolation

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Dependency — every Lambda function requires an IAM execution role whose trust policy names lambda.amazonaws.com; identity-based policies, resource-based policies, permissions boundaries, ABAC and IAM condition keys (lambda:FunctionUrlAuthType, lambda:SourceFunctionArn, lambda:VpcIds) govern all Lambda access. Creating a function also requires iam:PassRole.

Dependency — Lambda calls sts:AssumeRole on the function's execution role at invocation time to obtain temporary credentials injected into the execution environment; MicroVM build/execution roles require sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession.

Integration — AWS KMS provides encryption at rest for environment variables, .zip deployment packages, layer archives, event source mapping filter criteria, SnapStart snapshots and durable execution data, using either AWS owned/managed keys or a customer managed key (KMSKeyArn, Code.SourceKMSKeyArn, DurableConfig.KMSKeyArn, CapacityProvider KmsKeyArn).
Integration — CloudWatch Logs is the default destination for Lambda function and system logs; LoggingConfig controls the log group, JSON/Text format and application/system log levels.

Integration — Lambda publishes invocation, error, throttle, concurrency and code-signing metrics (e.g. SignatureValidationErrors) to CloudWatch, supports CloudWatch alarms, Lambda Insights, and CloudWatch Application Signals.
Integration — TracingConfig.Mode (Active/PassThrough) enables AWS X-Ray active tracing of function invocations; the execution role needs permission to upload trace data.

Integration — CloudTrail records Lambda control-plane API calls as management events and Invoke calls as data events for the AWS::Lambda::Function resource type; sensitive fields (Environment, ZipFile) are redacted.

Integration — Amazon S3 is a deployment-package source (Code.S3Bucket/S3Key, COPY or REFERENCE self-managed code storage), an event trigger (asynchronous invocation on object events), an S3 Batch Operations invocation target, a function log destination, and an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations and event source mappings.
Integration — Lambda FileSystemConfigs can mount an Amazon S3 Files access point at a /mnt/ path; the AWS::Lambda::Function CloudFormation create handler requires s3files:ListMountTargets.

Integration — container-image functions (PackageType=Image) reference an image URI in the Amazon ECR registry; Lambda creates an optimized copy encrypted with a separate key from the ECR image encryption.
Integration — Lambda FileSystemConfigs can mount an Amazon EFS access point for shared persistent state; the CloudFormation create handler requires elasticfilesystem:DescribeMountTargets.

Dependency/Integration — VPC-attached functions require Amazon EC2 network-interface permissions (Hyperplane ENIs) on the execution role plus subnets and security groups; interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) provide private inbound access to the Lambda API; Lambda Managed Instances capacity providers provision EC2 instance types; Amazon EC2 can also invoke Lambda functions.

Integration — Amazon SQS is an event source consumed via event source mappings, a dead-letter queue target (DeadLetterConfig.TargetArn), and an on-success/on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations and stream event sources.
Integration — Amazon SNS topics trigger asynchronous Lambda invocations, and are supported as dead-letter queue targets and as on-success/on-failure destinations.

Integration — Amazon DynamoDB Streams are consumed through event source mappings (with batch item failure reporting, tumbling windows, parallelization factor); DynamoDB is also a common target accessed via the execution role.
Integration — Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (stream or stream consumer ARNs) are consumed through event source mappings with error handling, on-failure destinations and stateful windowed processing.

Integration — Amazon Data Firehose can be configured as a Lambda function log destination for streaming to OpenSearch Service, Redshift Data API or third-party platforms; Firehose also invokes Lambda synchronously for record transformation.

Integration — Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka clusters (or MSK VPC connections for cross-account mappings) are consumed through event source mappings with IAM/SASL-SCRAM/mTLS cluster authentication, schema registry validation and provisioned event pollers.
Integration — Amazon MQ (ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ) brokers are consumed through event source mappings using BASIC_AUTH/VIRTUAL_HOST source access configurations backed by Secrets Manager.
Integration — Amazon DocumentDB change streams are consumed through event source mappings with database/collection scoping and FullDocument settings.

Integration — Amazon API Gateway synchronously invokes Lambda functions as the recommended way to publish a serverless backend, providing IAM/Cognito/Lambda authorizers, throttling and AWS WAF protection; it is the documented alternative to Lambda function URLs.

Integration — Amazon EventBridge event buses and rules invoke Lambda asynchronously (and EventBridge Pipes synchronously or asynchronously); an EventBridge event bus can also be an on-success/on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations.
Integration — Amazon EventBridge Pipes can invoke Lambda functions synchronously or asynchronously as pipe targets or enrichment steps.
Integration — Amazon EventBridge Scheduler invokes Lambda functions asynchronously on a time-based schedule (scheduled/periodic task use case).

Integration — AWS Step Functions invokes Lambda functions synchronously or asynchronously as workflow tasks; Lambda Durable Functions is documented as an alternative for long-running multi-step workflows.

Dependency — AWS Signer signing profiles are the trusted publishers referenced by a Lambda code signing configuration (AllowedPublishers.SigningProfileVersionArns); Lambda validates the signature at deployment time.

Integration — AWS Secrets Manager is the recommended store for credentials instead of environment variables, supplies Kafka/MQ/schema-registry authentication material for event source mappings, and invokes Lambda functions for secret rotation.

Integration — AWS Config records Lambda configuration items (AWS::Lambda::Function, AWS::Lambda::Alias, AWS::Lambda::CodeSigningConfig) for detective and preventative governance, and AWS Config asynchronously invokes Lambda functions to evaluate custom rules and perform remediation.

Integration — CloudFormation provisions 15 AWS::Lambda::* resource types (and AWS SAM's AWS::Serverless::Function transforms into them); CloudFormation also invokes Lambda functions asynchronously as custom resources, and CloudFormation Guard is recommended for proactive Lambda controls.

Integration — AWS Security Hub CSPM provides Lambda security controls (for example, validating that function resource-based policies prohibit public access), and Security Hub custom actions commonly invoke Lambda for automated remediation.

Integration — Amazon GuardDuty Lambda Protection monitors the network activity logs generated when Lambda functions are invoked to detect threats such as connections to malicious or cryptomining IP addresses.
Integration — Amazon Inspector automates security assessments (vulnerability scanning of function code and dependencies) for Lambda functions as part of the recommended governance strategy.

Integration — IAM Access Analyzer analyses external access to Lambda functions and function URLs and monitors for new or updated permissions that grant public or cross-account access; it also generates least-privilege execution role policies from CloudTrail activity.

Integration — AWS Organizations enables org-wide Lambda access control via aws:PrincipalOrgID/aws:PrincipalOrgPaths conditions in resource-based policies, PrincipalOrgID on AddPermission, organization-scoped layer sharing, and service control policies that constrain function URL auth types.

Integration — Amazon Cognito synchronously invokes Lambda functions as user pool triggers, and is the recommended identity provider (JWT issuance) for authenticating and authorizing users of publicly exposed Lambda-based workloads.
Integration — an Application Load Balancer can register a Lambda function as a target group and invokes it synchronously for HTTP(S) requests.
Integration — Amazon VPC Lattice invokes Lambda functions synchronously as service targets.
Integration — Lambda functions can be used with Kubernetes/Amazon EKS workloads as documented in the 'Integrating other services' chapter.
Integration — AWS IoT rules invoke Lambda functions asynchronously, supporting IoT backend use cases.
Integration — Amazon Simple Email Service invokes Lambda functions asynchronously (receipt rule actions).
Integration — Lambda functions connect to Amazon RDS databases (typically over a VPC attachment and with credentials from Secrets Manager), and Amazon RDS events can drive Lambda-based automation.

Integration — Amazon CloudFront can front a Lambda function URL or API endpoint (including origin access control to restrict direct access to the function URL) and absorb traffic spikes/DoS against public endpoints.
Integration — AWS WAF is recommended in front of Lambda-backed API endpoints to help protect against SQL injection, cross-site scripting and denial-of-service traffic.
Integration — AWS CodePipeline invokes Lambda functions asynchronously as custom pipeline actions.
Integration — AWS CodeCommit repository triggers invoke Lambda functions asynchronously.
Integration — Amazon Connect contact flows invoke Lambda functions synchronously to fetch or process data during a customer contact.

Sibling API surface — Lambda MicroVMs is the second Lambda compute primitive, exposed through its own API/CLI namespace (aws lambda-microvms) and CloudFormation types under AWS::Lambda (MicrovmImage, NetworkConnector), while sharing the lambda: IAM prefix, lambda.amazonaws.com service principal, and Firecracker isolation foundation.

entities.name: CapacityProvider
entities.overview:
A Lambda capacity provider defines a pool of Amazon EC2 compute that AWS Lambda provisions and operates on your behalf. It is the foundation for running Lambda functions on managed instances rather than on Lambda's default shared fleet. You declare where that compute runs, using VPC subnets and security groups, plus the IAM role Lambda assumes to manage instances.

The capacity provider also holds the compute preferences for the pool. You can restrict CPU architecture and instance types, cap total vCPUs, and choose automatic or manual scaling targets. Lambda handles instance provisioning, operating system and runtime patching, request routing, load balancing, and scaling.

A capacity provider acts as the trust boundary for the functions assigned to it. Functions attached to the same provider share underlying instances, so group only mutually trusted workloads together. Optional settings let you encrypt attached storage with your own AWS KMS key. You can also propagate tags to the instances, volumes, and network interfaces that Lambda creates. System logs for the pool go to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, where you choose the destination log group and level of detail.

entities.name: CodeSigningConfig
entities.overview:
An AWS Lambda code signing configuration is the trust definition behind Lambda code signing. It lists the AWS Signer signing profile versions that Lambda treats as trusted publishers, and it sets the action Lambda takes when a signature check fails. A single configuration can be attached to many functions, so a central team can define trust once and apply it broadly.

When a configuration is attached to a function, Lambda validates the signature of each new .zip deployment package and of each layer added to that function. The checks confirm that the artifact was signed by an allowed publisher, that its signature has not expired or been revoked, and that the artifact has not changed since signing. Validation runs at deployment time, so it does not affect function invocations. Functions packaged as container images are outside its scope.

The validation policy decides whether a failed check only raises a warning or blocks the deployment outright. Altered artifacts are always rejected. This design separates who defines trusted publishers from who ships code, which helps prevent tampered or unauthorized code from being deployed to a function even if deployment credentials are misused.

entities.name: DurableExecution
entities.overview:
A Lambda durable execution is a single long-running run of a durable Lambda function. It records progress as checkpoints so work survives interruptions. One execution can span many function invocations and continue for up to a year.

Lambda persists the execution's input payload, intermediate step results, callback results, and errors. When an execution resumes after a pause or a failure, Lambda replays the function from the start and substitutes the stored results for work already completed. This lets a workflow pause for timers, for an external system, or for a human approval without holding a running invocation.

Each execution carries its own identifier, status, and event history. You can inspect that history while the execution runs and after it reaches a terminal state, which gives you an audit trail for debugging and compliance review. Lambda deletes the history once the configured retention period elapses. A running execution can also be stopped, and an execution that is waiting on an external system can be completed, failed, or kept alive by that system.

entities.name: EventSourceMapping
entities.overview:
An event source mapping is a Lambda-managed poller that connects a stream or queue to a Lambda function. Lambda reads records from the source, groups them into batches, and invokes the function with each batch. This lets you consume messages from services that do not invoke functions directly, without running your own consumer fleet. Supported sources include Amazon SQS, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon DynamoDB Streams, Amazon MSK, self-managed Apache Kafka, Amazon MQ, and Amazon DocumentDB change streams.

The mapping is a separate Lambda resource with its own identifier, tags, and lifecycle, distinct from the function it targets. You control batching with a batch size and a batching window, and control throughput either by letting Lambda scale pollers automatically or by setting minimum and maximum provisioned pollers. Event filtering discards records that do not match your patterns before any invocation occurs. A mapping can be paused and resumed without losing its position in the source.

Configuration on the mapping also carries the connection details for the source. These include the source identifier or broker endpoints, the subnets and security group used to reach a private cluster, and references to stored secrets holding credentials or TLS certificates. Error handling options let you cap retries, discard records older than a chosen age, split failing batches, and route records that still fail to a separate queue, topic, or bucket for later inspection. Optional metrics and system logging give visibility into polling, filtering, invocation, and failure counts.

entities.name: Function
entities.overview:
An AWS Lambda function is a unit of serverless compute that runs your code in response to events or direct requests. You package handler code as a .zip archive or a container image, and Lambda provisions and manages the underlying execution environments. Lambda handles capacity, scaling, patching, and fault tolerance, so you do not maintain servers.

Each function carries its own configuration: memory and CPU allocation, timeout, instruction set architecture, environment variables, and language runtime. An IAM execution role defines which AWS resources the function code may reach. Optional settings attach the function to a virtual private cloud, mount shared file systems, size the temporary directory, and select customer managed encryption keys.

A function can publish immutable snapshots of its code and configuration, and route traffic through named pointers to those snapshots. This helps you roll out changes gradually and roll back quickly. Identity-based and resource-based policies control which principals, accounts, organizations, and AWS services may invoke it. Concurrency limits, asynchronous retry and destination settings, structured logging, and request tracing help you operate the function safely at scale.

entities.name: Layer
entities.overview:
An AWS Lambda layer is a .zip archive of supplementary code or data that functions can share. A layer typically holds library dependencies, a custom runtime, or configuration files. Moving those files out of the function deployment package keeps packages small and lets teams update shared dependencies independently of business logic.

Layers are published as numbered, immutable versions. Each version has its own Amazon Resource Name, and a function references the exact version it needs. When a function initializes, Lambda extracts the referenced layer contents into a directory that the language runtime searches, so the function can load the shared libraries or start a bundled extension.

A layer is private to the account that publishes it. The publisher can attach a permission statement to an individual layer version to allow use by another account, by all accounts in an organization, or by any AWS account. This makes layers a distribution mechanism for standardized dependencies, observability agents, and security tooling across many functions and accounts.

mitigations.statement: AWS Lambda service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: You can call the AWS Lambda API from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink. Calls over that network path can address Lambda resources in any account, including accounts outside your organization.

mitigations.statement: AWS Lambda service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: You can call the AWS Lambda API from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink. Calls over that network path can be made by IAM principals from any account, including accounts outside your organization.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should be configured to send system logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: A capacity provider produces system logs about the compute resources that Lambda provisions and manages for you. You can configure delivery of those logs to CloudWatch Logs on the capacity provider itself.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider's operator role should be assumed only by AWS Lambda acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your capacity provider's operator role, set through the `$.PermissionsConfig.CapacityProviderOperatorRoleArn` request parameter, has a trust policy that specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only AWS Lambda, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume this role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: You select the subnets for a capacity provider through `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]`. Private subnet placement helps reduce the network exposure of that capacity provider.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should use an EC2 instance type that supports automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

mitigationContext.context: A capacity provider runs your function code on Amazon EC2 instances placed in your own VPC. The instance type backing that pool determines whether traffic to other instances you operate is automatically encrypted in the Nitro System hardware.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: A capacity provider accepts a KMS key ARN through `$.KmsKeyArn`, which encrypts the Amazon EBS storage on the Managed Instances it provisions. When you omit this parameter, encryption defaults to an AWS managed key instead of a key you control.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should launch its instances in subnets in more than one Availability Zone

mitigationContext.context: A capacity provider defines the VPC subnets where Lambda launches and manages the instances that run your functions. Lambda creates and attaches network interfaces for those instances, placing them in the Availability Zones of those subnets.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: A capacity provider is a durably persisted, account-level resource with its own ARN, so it supports resource tagging directly. Tags that record owner and purpose help you identify who is accountable for each compute pool.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda capacity provider should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: You supply security groups for a capacity provider through `$.VpcConfig.SecurityGroupIds[*]`. Those groups control network access for the compute instances that run your function code.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda code signing config should only be configured with a trusted AWS Signer signing profile version

mitigationContext.context: A code signing config sets its allowed publishers through `$.AllowedPublishers.SigningProfileVersionArns[*]`. Each entry names an AWS Signer signing profile version that can belong to a different account.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda code signing config should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: A code signing config is a durable, independently addressable Lambda resource with its own Amazon Resource Name. Lambda supports native tags on this resource to record owner and purpose information.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping should be configured to send system logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping supports system-level logging for its event pollers, with those records delivered to CloudWatch Logs. Each mapping has its own log stream for reviewing poller behavior.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping can reach a private event source through network interfaces that Lambda places in your VPC subnets. This network placement belongs to the mapping itself, and is separate from the target function's VPC configuration.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping's filter criteria should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping can hold a filter criteria object that determines which records Lambda passes to your function. By default, that object is not encrypted with a key that you manage.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping should have Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping supports a VPC subnet source access configuration for connecting to your event source. That configuration determines the Availability Zones of the mapping's network interfaces.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping is a persistent AWS Lambda resource that supports tags on its own ARN. It does not inherit tags from the function it invokes.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping should have the `EventCount`, `ErrorCount`, and `KafkaMetrics` event source mapping metric groups enabled to collect detailed CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping supports an opt-in metrics configuration offering the `EventCount`, `ErrorCount`, and `KafkaMetrics` metric groups. Lambda publishes the groups you select to CloudWatch.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda event source mapping should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: An event source mapping for a self-managed Apache Kafka cluster can include your VPC security groups as `VPC_SECURITY_GROUP` source access configurations. These groups control inbound and outbound traffic on the network interfaces that Lambda creates for the mapping.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be configured to send application and system logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: A Lambda function runs your code and emits both application and system logs that it can send to CloudWatch Logs. System logs record per-invocation activity, and application logs carry the diagnostic output your code emits.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function's execution role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Your function calls AWS services using the IAM execution role you specify through the `$.Role` request parameter. Lambda provides that role's temporary credentials to your function code during each invocation.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function's IAM execution role should be assumed only by AWS Lambda acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your Lambda function's IAM execution role, set through the `$.Role` request parameter, has a trust policy you author to control who can assume it. Allowing only AWS Lambda, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: You attach a function to subnets in your VPC through `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]`, so subnet placement is a property you control on the function itself. Because you choose those subnets, you can limit a function's placement to private subnets.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: AWS Lambda API calls against your function can arrive from your VPCs and on-premises networks or from unexpected networks. Restricting where requests to your function originate from enforces the network perimeter and helps keep your function accessible only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted AWS Lambda function resources

mitigationContext.context: Your identities can direct AWS Lambda API calls, including invocations, at function ARNs in accounts outside your organization. The resource perimeter objective is that your identities can access only trusted resources.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be in an Amazon VPC

mitigationContext.context: By default, an AWS Lambda function runs outside your VPC with public internet access. VPC attachment is an optional, reversible part of a function's configuration.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: A Lambda function accepts customer managed key identifiers directly on its own create and update operations. These keys encrypt the function's environment variables, SnapStart snapshots, .zip deployment package, optimized container image, and durable execution payload data.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should have Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

mitigationContext.context: When you connect a function to a VPC, Lambda creates a Hyperplane ENI for each subnet and security group combination you configure. The subnets you list in `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]` therefore determine which Availability Zones those network interfaces occupy.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function's resource-based policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: An AWS Lambda function has its own resource-based policy that grants IAM principals permission to invoke it. This policy can be written to grant invoke access to all IAM principals rather than a named subset.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should not allow unauthenticated access through its function URL or resource-based policy

mitigationContext.context: A Lambda function can expose a function URL, a dedicated HTTPS endpoint whose `$.AuthType` setting controls whether Lambda authenticates callers. That setting and your function's resource-based policy together determine whether identities outside your organization can invoke your function.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your Lambda function supports a resource-based policy that defines which identities and AWS services can invoke or manage it. Because access to the function is authorized through IAM, you can restrict it to trusted identities.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be accessed by an AWS service principal, such as the Amazon S3 service principal, only when the service principal is acting on behalf of a trusted resource, AWS account, or organization

mitigationContext.context: You can attach a resource-based policy to an AWS Lambda function that grants an AWS service principal permission to invoke it. A grant to a service principal alone does not identify the resource or account the service is acting on behalf of.

mitigations.statement: Permissions to generate presigned URLs signed by the AWS Lambda service principal that grant access to a Lambda function's deployment package should be restricted to select principals

mitigationContext.context: `GetFunction` returns an Amazon S3 presigned URL for downloading your function's deployment package from a service-owned bucket. The presigned URL is created with an AWS Lambda service principal identity, and you cannot apply a bucket policy to that AWS-managed bucket.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag a Lambda function when you call `CreateFunction` or later by calling `TagResource` with the function ARN. Tagging each function with owner and purpose values helps you attribute it to a responsible team and project.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should have CloudWatch Lambda Insights enhanced monitoring and CloudWatch Application Signals enabled to collect detailed CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Amazon CloudWatch Lambda Insights can publish system-level metrics, such as CPU time, memory, `/tmp` disk, and network usage, beyond your function's default invocation metrics. Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals can also publish request-level metrics that the default metrics do not include.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda function should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: A Lambda function that connects to your VPC is associated with security groups you choose through `$.VpcConfig.SecurityGroupIds[*]`. Those groups control the network traffic allowed for your function, including the outbound connections it initiates.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted AWS Lambda layer resources

mitigationContext.context: Layer versions can be shared and consumed by other accounts, so your identities can read or attach one owned outside your organization. A resource perimeter helps your identities access only trusted resources: those owned by your AWS accounts or by AWS services acting on your behalf.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda layer should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: A Lambda layer version can carry its own resource-based policy that grants layer usage permission to other accounts. That policy accepts a wildcard principal covering all AWS accounts.

mitigations.statement: An AWS Lambda layer should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Each version of your layer carries its own resource-based policy that can grant other accounts permission to retrieve the layer archive. Sharing can also extend to every account in an organization, or to all AWS accounts.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make AWS Lambda service API calls

threatContext.context: An IAM principal from outside your organization can use the interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink) in your VPC with its own credentials. That access enables transfer of data from your VPC to Lambda resources in an AWS account outside your organization.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted AWS Lambda resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: A principal on your VPC network can reach AWS Lambda functions and layer versions in accounts outside your organization. That access enables invoking a cross-account function with your data as input or downloading its deployment package and layer archives.
`GetLayerVersion` might require access to service-owned layers, which are layers that are managed in service accounts.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify data in an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the Amazon EBS volumes of the Managed Instances that Lambda provisions for the capacity provider with key material inaccessible to the AWS account owner

threatContext.context: An IAM principal that creates your capacity provider selects the encryption key for the Amazon EBS volumes of its Managed Instances. If that key material sits outside your control, its holder can later revoke or delete it and leave those volumes unrecoverable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can configure the capacity provider without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An AWS Lambda capacity provider is an account-level resource that supports tagging at creation and afterwards. An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify one can omit required tags and may leave the resource without ownership attribution.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the capacity provider with an AWS managed KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify a capacity provider can encrypt its data with an AWS managed KMS key. You cannot change an AWS managed key's policy or govern its lifecycle.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can create the capacity provider in a single Availability Zone

threatContext.context: `CreateCapacityProvider` accepts as few as one subnet in the VPC configuration subnet list, `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]`. A capacity provider confined to one Availability Zone may become unavailable to the function versions bound to it during a zonal impairment.

threats.prerequisites: who controls a VPC-connected resource in the same VPC as an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can interact with the capacity provider's Managed Instance network interfaces over HTTPS or HTTP through overly permissive network rules and move laterally within the VPC

threatContext.context: Your capacity provider launches Amazon EC2 Managed Instances with network interfaces in the VPC subnets you specify. A threat actor controlling another resource in that VPC can reach those interfaces through overly permissive network rules and move laterally.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an AWS Lambda capacity provider that permits traffic to services and administrative ports from unrestricted sources
threats.threatAction: can reach listening services and administrative ports on the compute instances managed by the capacity provider

threatContext.context: Security groups associated with a capacity provider admit inbound traffic to the Amazon EC2 instances that run your function code. An inbound rule permitting an unrestricted source range makes listening services and administrative ports on those instances reachable over the network.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an AWS Lambda capacity provider that has been placed in a public subnet
threats.threatAction: can access the capacity provider directly from an ungoverned network

threatContext.context: A capacity provider launches Amazon EC2 managed instances and their network interfaces into the subnets you choose at creation time. If you choose a public subnet, a threat actor may be able to access the capacity provider directly from an ungoverned network.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or update an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can configure the capacity provider to use an EC2 instance type that does not provide automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

threatContext.context: A capacity provider's allowed instance types setting (`$.InstanceRequirements.AllowedInstanceTypes[*]`) accepts Amazon EC2 instance types that do not provide automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic. If such a type is selected, traffic between the capacity provider's instances and other instances you operate can travel without that encryption.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my AWS Lambda capacity provider's operator IAM role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my operator role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Every AWS Lambda capacity provider designates an operator role whose trust policy you author yourself. That trust policy can allow an untrusted principal to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an AWS Lambda capacity provider
threats.threatAction: can disable system logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for the capacity provider

threatContext.context: The create and update operations for a capacity provider both accept the CloudWatch log group destination for system logs, `$.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.LogGroup`. A principal able to modify a capacity provider can use that setting to end system log delivery to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

threats.prerequisites: with control of an AWS Lambda capacity provider configured with overly permissive outbound security group rules
threats.threatAction: can use the capacity provider to interact with ungoverned network destinations

threatContext.context: Outbound rules on the security groups attached to a capacity provider control which destinations its network traffic can reach. Where those rules permit unrestricted outbound traffic, the capacity provider can interact with ungoverned network destinations.

threats.prerequisites: who can execute code in an AWS Lambda capacity provider that is attached to a subnet with a route to an internet gateway
threats.threatAction: can send the capacity provider's outbound traffic directly to the public internet instead of through a governed network egress path

threatContext.context: All egress from functions on a capacity provider leaves through managed Amazon EC2 instance network interfaces in the subnets you specify. Where those subnets route to an internet gateway, code running on the pool can reach the public internet directly.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify my AWS Lambda code signing config
threats.threatAction: can configure my code signing config to use an untrusted AWS Signer signing profile version to validate the signature of code packages and layers deployed to the functions that reference the configuration

threatContext.context: An IAM principal that can create or modify your code signing config sets its allowed publishers list (`$.AllowedPublishers.SigningProfileVersionArns[*]`). At deployment time, AWS Lambda validates code packages and layers against those AWS Signer signing profiles, including any owned by accounts outside your organization.

`CreateCodeSigningConfig` allows you to specify a signing profile that does not belong to your organization as the value for the `AllowedPublishers.SigningProfileVersionArns` request parameter. Because the subsequent call against the signing profile is performed by the service principal, it is not restricted with `aws:ResourceOrgID` implemented in a service control policy.

`UpdateCodeSigningConfig` allows you to specify an AWS Signer signing profile that does not belong to your organization as the value for the `AllowedPublishers.SigningProfileVersionArns` request parameter. Because the subsequent call against the AWS Signer signing profile is performed by the service principal, it is not restricted with `aws:ResourceOrgID` implemented in a service control policy.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda code signing config
threats.threatAction: can configure the code signing config without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal can create a Lambda code signing configuration without tags, and call `UntagResource` to remove tag keys from one already tagged. The configuration then could carry no required owner or purpose tag, yet it still decides which signing profiles are trusted to sign your function code.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping that is not attached to a VPC
threats.threatAction: can use the event source mapping to send and receive traffic outside the network controls a VPC would enforce by pointing the poller at publicly reachable brokers, schema registries, or on-failure destinations

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping can omit its VPC subnet and security group configuration. Its event pollers can send and receive traffic outside the network controls a VPC would enforce, reaching public brokers, schema registries, and on-failure destinations.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping
threats.threatAction: can disable the `EventCount`, `ErrorCount`, and `KafkaMetrics` metric groups for the event source mapping

threatContext.context: The `EventCount`, `ErrorCount`, and `KafkaMetrics` metric groups determine the detailed CloudWatch metrics an event source mapping publishes. A principal calling `UpdateEventSourceMapping` can remove those groups from the mapping.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the filter criteria object with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal that can create or modify your event source mapping sets `$.KMSKeyArn`, the customer managed key encrypting its filter criteria. That principal can name a key you do not administer, taking control of the key policy, its lifecycle, and decryption of the stored criteria.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping
threats.threatAction: can configure the event source mapping without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An event source mapping is a taggable AWS Lambda resource that an IAM principal with create or modify permissions can configure without required tags. An untagged mapping may not be covered by your ownership attribution and cost allocation processes.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping's filter criteria
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the filter criteria with an AWS owned KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle and to audit key usage through CloudTrail

threatContext.context: A principal that creates or modifies an event source mapping's filter criteria can leave them encrypted under an AWS owned key outside your account. You cannot then govern that key's permissions, rotation, or deletion, or audit its use.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping that supports detailed CloudWatch metrics through the `EventCount`, `ErrorCount`, and `KafkaMetrics` event source mapping metric groups
threats.threatAction: can create or configure the event source mapping without any event source mapping metric group enabled

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify your event source mapping can leave the `EventCount`, `ErrorCount`, and `KafkaMetrics` metric groups unselected. The mapping then runs without the detailed stage-level poller measurements those groups publish.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping
threats.threatAction: can create or modify the event source mapping with subnets that all resolve to a single Availability Zone, placing the event poller's network interfaces in that one Availability Zone

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an event source mapping can select subnets that all resolve to a single Availability Zone. Impairment of that zone can then interrupt polling and downstream function invocation.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read the filter patterns from an AWS Lambda event source mapping's filter criteria that has not been encrypted at rest with a KMS customer managed key
threats.threatAction: can read plaintext filter patterns and the business values they embed in the filter criteria

threatContext.context: An event source mapping stores filter criteria patterns that can embed literal business values. A principal holding only `lambda:GetEventSourceMapping` or `lambda:ListEventSourceMappings` permission can read those patterns in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an AWS Lambda event source mapping
threats.threatAction: can interact with the event source mapping without a record of their activities being persisted by event poller system logging to CloudWatch Logs

threatContext.context: System logging for event pollers is optional, so your event source mapping can operate without sending poller logs to CloudWatch Logs. A threat actor can then create, change, disable, or delete the mapping without those poller activities being persisted.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read the filter patterns from an AWS Lambda event source mapping's filter criteria that has been encrypted with an AWS owned KMS key
threats.threatAction: can read the filter patterns in the filter criteria

threatContext.context: By default, your event source mapping's filter criteria is encrypted at rest with an AWS owned key. An IAM principal with unintended read permissions can retrieve the stored filter patterns in plaintext.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an AWS Lambda event source mapping
threats.threatAction: can disable system logging to CloudWatch Logs for the event source mapping

threatContext.context: Permissions to modify your event source mapping extend to the system log delivery it configures for Amazon CloudWatch Logs. A principal that can disable that delivery can leave subsequent event poller activity unrecorded at the resource level.

threats.prerequisites: with control of an AWS Lambda event source mapping configured with overly permissive outbound security group rules
threats.threatAction: can use the event source mapping to interact with ungoverned network destinations, directing its event poller's outbound connections and the record batches they carry to endpoints outside the intended network boundary

threatContext.context: Your event source mapping's pollers carry polled record batches over outbound connections from network interfaces in your subnets. Overly permissive outbound rules on the security groups you author let those connections reach destinations beyond your intended network boundary.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create, modify or invoke an AWS Lambda function that is not attached to a VPC
threats.threatAction: can use the function to send and receive traffic outside the network controls a VPC would enforce

threatContext.context: Your function does not run in your VPCs when `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]` and `$.VpcConfig.SecurityGroupIds[*]` are empty. An IAM principal with create, modify, or invoke permissions can then use it to send and receive traffic on unexpected networks, including the public internet.
`CreateFunction` allows you to associate functions with an Amazon VPC to run your code.
`UpdateFunctionConfiguration` allows you to associate functions with an Amazon VPC to run your code.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an AWS Lambda function or its execution role
threats.threatAction: can disable CloudWatch Lambda Insights enhanced monitoring, CloudWatch Application Signals, and AWS X-Ray active tracing for the function

threatContext.context: CloudWatch Lambda Insights enhanced monitoring, CloudWatch Application Signals, and AWS X-Ray active tracing are opt-in features you enable on a Lambda function. An IAM principal with permissions to modify the function or its execution role can turn this monitoring off.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify data in an AWS Lambda function
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the function's environment variables, .zip deployment package, SnapStart snapshots, and durable execution payload data with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: `$.KMSKeyArn`, `$.Code.SourceKMSKeyArn`, and `$.DurableConfig.KMSKeyArn` accept any symmetric customer managed key ARN, including keys backed by external or imported key material. A principal that creates or updates the function can therefore bind its encrypted state to key material the account owner cannot administer.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda function
threats.threatAction: can configure the function without required tagging information

threatContext.context: Lambda applies tags at the function level, so the function itself is the taggable unit. A principal that creates or modifies a function without your required tags leaves it outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda function
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the function with an AWS owned or AWS managed KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle

threatContext.context: A principal able to create or modify a function can have the function's state encrypted under an AWS owned or AWS managed key. Both key classes reduce your control over the key's lifecycle and policy, and an AWS owned key leaves you no key-usage audit trail.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public AWS Lambda functions, or prior knowledge of an existing public function
threats.threatAction: can access a function that has been configured to allow public access, either through a function URL that permits unauthenticated invocation or through a resource-based policy that grants a wildcard principal, and invoke the function or read its configuration

threatContext.context: A function URL that allows unauthenticated access, or a resource-based policy with a wildcard principal, exposes your function to callers outside your account. A threat actor who discovers the function can then invoke it or read its configuration.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda function that supports CloudWatch Lambda Insights enhanced monitoring and CloudWatch Application Signals
threats.threatAction: can create or configure the function without CloudWatch Lambda Insights enhanced monitoring or CloudWatch Application Signals enabled

threatContext.context: A function can be created and invoked with only the default invocation metrics, such as counts, errors, and duration. Without CloudWatch Lambda Insights system-level measurements or CloudWatch Application Signals latency and fault metrics, anomalous resource use may be harder to detect.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to invoke, modify, or delete an untrusted AWS Lambda function
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted function, including sending data to it in the invocation payload or receiving data from it in the invocation response

threatContext.context: The function name or ARN on `Invoke`, `$.FunctionName`, can address a function in an account outside your organization. Your principal can then send sensitive data to that function in the invocation payload, `$.Payload`, and receive data in its response.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an AWS Lambda function
threats.threatAction: can create the function in a single Availability Zone by attaching it to VPC subnets that all resolve to one zone

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify your function can attach it to VPC subnets that all reside in one Availability Zone. An impairment of that zone can then disrupt the function's network path, making the workload it serves unavailable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use my AWS Lambda function and access to an unexpected network
threats.threatAction: can interact with my function from an unexpected network

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to use your function can invoke, modify, or delete it from an unexpected network. AWS Lambda API calls against your function can succeed from unexpected networks as well as from your expected networks.
`AddPermission` allows you to apply a resource-based policy to grant access to a function. The service currently does not support resource control policies.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read environment variables, deployment package code and durable execution payloads from an AWS Lambda function that has not been encrypted at rest with a KMS customer managed key
threats.threatAction: can read plaintext environment variables, deployment package code and durable execution payloads in the function

threatContext.context: The function's environment variables, deployment package, and durable execution payloads can be encrypted under default keys you do not govern. `GetFunction`, `GetFunctionConfiguration`, and `GetDurableExecution` then return that data in plaintext to any principal holding those read permissions.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my AWS Lambda function through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: can use my function, invoking it with a chosen `$.Payload` and `$.Qualifier` to run my code under its execution role, reading its environment variables and deployment package with `GetFunction`, replacing what it runs with `UpdateFunctionCode`, or deleting it

threatContext.context: A resource-based policy on a Lambda function can grant actions such as `lambda:InvokeFunction`, `lambda:GetFunction`, and `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` to an IAM principal outside your organization. That principal can then run your code under the execution role, read the environment variables and deployment package, or replace that code.
`AddPermission` allows you to apply a resource-based policy to grant access to a function. The service currently does not support resource control policies.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my AWS Lambda function's IAM execution role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my execution role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: You author the trust policy of the IAM execution role that Lambda assumes for your function. Principals outside your organization that the trust policy names may be able to assume the execution role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with possession of credentials for my AWS Lambda function execution role
threats.threatAction: can use my function execution role while on an unexpected network

threatContext.context: AWS Lambda generates temporary credentials by assuming the IAM execution role you specify in the `$.Role` request parameter. A threat actor who obtains those credentials can use that execution role while on an unexpected network.

`CreateFunction` allows you to specify a service role, referred to as the function's execution role, for your Lambda function operations. The service uses the role to make AWS API calls from your code.

`UpdateFunctionConfiguration` allows you to specify a service role, referred to as the function's execution role, for your Lambda function operations. The service uses the role to make AWS API calls from your code.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read environment variables from an AWS Lambda function that is encrypted with an AWS managed KMS key in the same account as the principal
threats.threatAction: can read the environment variables in the function

threatContext.context: By default, your function's environment variables are encrypted with the `aws/lambda` AWS managed key. A same-account IAM principal with unintended read permissions on the function receives those variables already decrypted in the `GetFunctionConfiguration` response.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read the .zip deployment package and function configuration details from an AWS Lambda function that has been encrypted with an AWS owned KMS key
threats.threatAction: can read the .zip deployment package and function configuration details in the function

threatContext.context: By default, your function's .zip deployment package and configuration details are encrypted with an AWS owned KMS key. A principal holding `lambda:GetFunction` or `lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration` on the function can retrieve that code and those configuration details.

threats.prerequisites: with access to configure an AWS service that has been granted access to an AWS Lambda function through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: may be able to cause that AWS service to interact with the function using the principal's data or context

threatContext.context: Your function's resource-based policy may grant `lambda:InvokeFunction` to AWS service principals such as `s3.amazonaws.com` or `sns.amazonaws.com`. A principal in another account can configure that service to invoke your function with event payloads they control.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an AWS Lambda function
threats.threatAction: can disable CloudWatch Logs delivery of system and application logs for the function

threatContext.context: A principal with permissions to modify your function can stop delivery of its system and application logs to CloudWatch Logs. Invocations continue to run while no log records are delivered for that later activity.

threats.prerequisites: with permissions to read an AWS Lambda function, which returns an Amazon S3 presigned URL signed by the AWS Lambda service principal for a service-owned bucket
threats.threatAction: can use the presigned URL to read the function's deployment package's data in the service-owned bucket while on an unexpected network

threatContext.context: Calling `GetFunction` for the function named in `$.FunctionName` returns an Amazon S3 presigned URL that AWS Lambda creates with a service principal identity. Anyone in possession of the URL can download your function's deployment package from a service-owned bucket without further authorization.

`GetFunction` returns an Amazon S3 presigned URL that users can use to download AWS Lambda function deployment packages from service-owned buckets. The presigned URL is created with the AWS Lambda service principal.

threats.prerequisites: with control of an AWS Lambda function configured with overly permissive outbound security group rules
threats.threatAction: can use the function to interact with ungoverned network destinations

threatContext.context: A threat actor who controls a VPC-attached function can run code that opens outbound network connections. When an outbound security group rule permits an unrestricted destination range, those connections can reach arbitrary external endpoints.

threats.prerequisites: who can execute code in an AWS Lambda function that is attached to a subnet with a route to an internet gateway
threats.threatAction: can send the function's outbound traffic directly to the public internet instead of through a governed network egress path

threatContext.context: A threat actor able to execute code in a function can open outbound connections from the subnets you attach it to. If that subnet's route table has a route to an internet gateway, the traffic reaches the public internet outside a governed egress path.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public AWS Lambda layers, or prior knowledge of an existing public layer
threats.threatAction: can access a layer that has been configured to allow public access, reading the layer version and retrieving a download link to its .zip archive, or attaching the layer version to a function in their own account

threatContext.context: A layer version can be configured to allow public access. Any AWS account holder who discovers its ARN can then download the layer archive or attach the layer to their own function.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to read, use, or modify an untrusted AWS Lambda layer
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted layer, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: When an account outside your organization shares a layer version with you, your IAM principals can call `GetLayerVersion` or `GetLayerVersionByArn` to download its archive. If they pass that layer version in `$.Layers[*]` on `CreateFunction` or `UpdateFunctionConfiguration`, AWS Lambda extracts its contents into your function's execution environment.
`GetLayerVersion` might require access to service-owned layers, which are layers that are managed in service accounts.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my AWS Lambda layer through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: can use my layer to download the layer archive and to attach the layer version to functions in accounts I do not control

threatContext.context: The resource-based policy on your Lambda layer version can name another account, the account root user, or a wildcard principal. An identity outside your organization with that grant can call `GetLayerVersion` to download the archive, or add the version to a function it controls.
`AddLayerVersionPermission` allows you to apply a resource-based policy to grant access to a layer version. The service currently does not support resource control policies.

implementationContext.context: This policy enforces `aws:ResourceOrgID` to match your organization for AWS Lambda service API calls made through your interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink). Requests from that network to Lambda resources outside your organization are denied, except for the AWS-owned Lambda layer ARNs you explicitly list.

Some AWS services publish Lambda extensions as layers owned by an AWS service account. That account sits outside your organization, so `aws:ResourceOrgID` does not match requests to those layers. List the service-owned layer ARNs in a separate statement, scoped with `aws:PrincipalOrgID`. This keeps your functions able to consume those layers while the resource perimeter stays in place.

implementationContext.context: This implementation validates `$.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.LogGroup` and `$.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.SystemLogLevel` before a capacity provider is created. Requiring a declared log group and a log level that keeps the needed detail helps preserve capacity provider system logs for investigating activity on your managed instances.

This implementation records `UpdateCapacityProvider` and `CreateCapacityProvider` calls that set `$.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.LogGroup`, your log group destination, and `$.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.SystemLogLevel`, your system log level. Recording these calls helps you detect an unintended or unexpected change to your capacity provider logging configuration.

This periodic rule enumerates your capacity providers and reads `$.CapacityProvider.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.LogGroup` and `$.CapacityProvider.TelemetryConfig.LoggingConfig.SystemLogLevel`. It flags providers that do not send system logs to your intended log group and detail level, helping preserve visibility into managed instance activity.

This implementation reads `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`, the trust policy of the operator role named in `$.PermissionsConfig.CapacityProviderOperatorRoleArn`. Creation of the capacity provider fails when that trust policy grants public access, or grants role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain.

The reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

Flagging a trust policy that can grant public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, helps you detect over-permissive grants.

implementationContext.context: This implementation guidance recommends a trust policy on `$.PermissionsConfig.CapacityProviderOperatorRoleArn`, your capacity provider operator role, that restricts assumption to the AWS Lambda service principal `lambda.amazonaws.com`.

Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires.

This implementation governs `sts:AssumeRole` through the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key, while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. As a result, principals outside your organization are restricted from assuming the capacity provider operator role at `$.PermissionsConfig.CapacityProviderOperatorRoleArn`.

To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation validates each subnet in `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]` at create time, resolving that subnet's route table for a default route to an internet gateway. Subnets carrying that route fail validation, so your capacity provider instances are not placed in public subnets as determined by that test.

This periodic check reads `$.CapacityProvider.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]`, the subnets where your capacity provider launches compute instances, then resolves each subnet's route table. It flags a default route whose gateway target (`$.RouteTables[*].Routes[*].GatewayId`) is an internet gateway, surfacing capacity providers configured with internet-routable subnets.

This hook validates `$.InstanceRequirements.AllowedInstanceTypes[*]` at create time, so a capacity provider permitting instance types without automatic instance-to-instance encryption is not created. That helps provide an additional layer of encryption in transit between your Managed Instances without application changes.

This check compares the allowed instance types of your AWS Lambda capacity provider at `$.CapacityProvider.InstanceRequirements.AllowedInstanceTypes[*]` with EC2 encryption-in-transit support at `$.instanceTypeSet[*].networkInfo.encryptionInTransitSupported`. It flags a capacity provider that can launch instance types without automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic.

This implementation validates `$.KmsKeyArn`, the KMS key ARN that encrypts your capacity provider's resources, in CloudFormation stack operations. Requiring your own key at create time helps address the mitigation by giving you control over the key lifecycle and permissions.

This periodic check reads `$.CapacityProvider.KmsKeyArn` for each capacity provider and resolves the referenced key through `$.KeyMetadata.KeyManager`. It flags capacity providers whose managed instance volumes fall back to an AWS managed key, helping you retain control of key policy and rotation.

Configure your capacity provider's VpcConfig.SubnetIds with two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Spanning at least two zones helps network connectivity for your functions survive the loss of a single zone.

Availability Zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the capacity provider. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 DescribeSubnets operation and confirm that the AvailabilityZone field differs across the subnets you chose. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so the templates and modules that create capacity providers supply at least two subnets from different zones. Do this at create time, because UpdateCapacityProvider does not accept VpcConfig. Changing the network placement of a live capacity provider requires replacing it.

To verify the deployed state, call GetCapacityProvider and review the subnet IDs it returns. You can also enumerate the attached network interfaces with the Amazon EC2 DescribeNetworkInterfaces operation. Confirm that their subnets span more than one zone. Note that Lambda hides managed instances and their network interfaces from Amazon EC2 list operations by default. The account-level managed resource visibility setting controls this behavior, and direct queries by resource ID still return hidden managed resources.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Add the application resources that depend on your capacity provider to a Resilience Hub application. Run a resiliency assessment, which flags single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy.

implementationContext.context: This recommendation directs you to supply `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]` values drawn from two or more Availability Zones. guidance.description:
Associate your capacity provider only with security groups that restrict network access for the Lambda Managed Instances compute instances. Configure those security groups following least-privilege best practices. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the sources and destinations, protocols, and ports that your functions require. Sources and destinations can be IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any IP address, particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. If you omit `SecurityGroupIds`, Lambda uses the default security group for your VPC. Specify your own purpose-built security groups instead. Because a change to the VPC configuration requires replacing the capacity provider, choose these security groups before you create it.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope a policy by account, organizational unit, or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group to in-scope resources. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow-list or a block-list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate them. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope that describes the access you consider unintended. For example, describe any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Run an analysis with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope` and `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, then review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

This implementation flags functions whose recorded `$.configuration.vpcConfig.subnetIds[*]` and `$.configuration.vpcConfig.securityGroupIds[*]` are empty. Attaching your function to a VPC helps address the mitigation by placing its network reachability under your own subnet and security group controls.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `lambda:VpcIds` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `lambda:CreateFunction` and `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration`. These conditions help prevent principals in your organization from deploying functions without a VPC attachment, while exempting principals you tag for exclusion (`aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude`).

Restricting function deployment to a VPC you manage is a data perimeter control for AWS Lambda. Functions without a VPC attachment reach the internet over a network path your VPC does not control. Requiring the `lambda:VpcIds` condition key on function create and update calls brings that traffic into your VPC. You can then inspect it by using VPC endpoint policies and network perimeter controls.
