implementationContext.context: This hook restricts your function's KMS key properties (`$.KmsKeyArn`, `$.Code.SourceKMSKeyArn`, `$.DurableConfig.KMSKeyArn`) to keys that `DescribeKey` identifies as customer managed. Create and update requests that do not satisfy that condition are denied, which helps keep the key policy and lifecycle under your control.

This rule resolves `$.KeyMetadata.KeyManager` for the key recorded at `$.configuration.kmskeyArn`, the key that encrypts your function's environment variables and SnapStart snapshots. A function is flagged as noncompliant when that key is not customer managed, identifying functions whose encryption key you do not manage.

guidance.description:
Configure your Lambda function's VPC subnet list with two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. This recommendation applies to functions you attach to a VPC in your account. A function with no VPC configuration is already available across Availability Zones in the Region.

The Hyperplane elastic network interfaces (ENIs) that Lambda creates for your function are tied to the subnet and security group combination you supply. Supplying subnets from more than one Availability Zone places those ENIs in more than one zone. This helps your function's VPC network connectivity survive the loss of a single zone.

Subnet-to-Availability-Zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the function. A subnet resides entirely within one Availability Zone and cannot span zones. Before you supply subnet IDs, confirm that they belong to distinct Availability Zones. The Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation returns the `AvailabilityZone` field for each subnet. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so the templates and modules that create your functions always supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, check the subnet placement your function reports through `GetFunctionConfiguration` under `VpcConfig.SubnetIds`. You can also enumerate network interfaces with the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation. Lambda manages the Hyperplane ENIs and they are not directly visible to you, so the function's own configuration is the more direct check. Confirm that the subnets span more than one Availability Zone.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your function among an application's resources in Resilience Hub and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment flags single-Availability-Zone concentration against your resiliency policy.

implementationContext.context: This recommendation has you supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in your function's VPC subnet configuration. Spreading the Hyperplane ENIs Lambda creates for your function across zones helps VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

This hook validates at create and update time that `$.VpcConfig.SubnetIds[*]` lists two or more subnet entries. Requiring more than one subnet entry is the precondition for placing your function's network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone.

This implementation reads `$.configuration.vpcConfig.subnetIds[*]` on your function, then resolves each subnet's `$.subnetSet[*].availabilityZone`. It flags a VPC-connected function confined to one Availability Zone, addressing the mitigation by surfacing single-zone Hyperplane ENI placement.

This implementation restricts invoke and read access to your function with the `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition key. Requests from IAM principals outside the defined subset are denied, which helps protect your function from unintended access.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to authorized identities. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This hook restricts create and update requests for your Lambda permissions that grant an action (`$.Action`) to a wildcard principal (`$.Principal`). These requests are denied unless the permission also sets an organization ID (`$.PrincipalOrgID`), a source account (`$.SourceAccount`), or a source ARN (`$.SourceArn`).

This hook calls the AWS IAM Access Analyzer `CheckNoPublicAccess` custom policy check with your permission statement as `$.policyDocument`. The check uses automated reasoning to determine whether the statement might grant public access. Requests to create or update the permission are denied unless the check returns a `$.result` of `PASS`.

links.title: AWS IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks

implementationContext.context: This implementation evaluates the `$.PolicyDocument` declared for your Lambda function and rejects a policy that can grant public access. Requiring explicit principals instead of a wildcard helps prevent your function from inadvertently becoming invocable by unintended principals.

This implementation recommends using Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (CheckNoPublicAccess) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance, provably verifying that a policy does not grant public access.

links.title: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks

implementationContext.context: This rule reads your function's resource-based policy from `$.supplementaryConfiguration.Policy` and marks the function noncompliant when the public-access check returns a `$.result` other than `PASS`. That verdict surfaces policies that may allow public access, helping you replace broad grants with explicit principal definitions.

This implementation evaluates the policy document with the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy check `CheckNoPublicAccess`. The check applies automated reasoning to the policy you pass to it. A `PASS` result means the policy does not allow public access for the resource type. A `FAIL` result means the policy might allow public access. The check also reports the policy statements behind that result, so you can review them.

links.title: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks

implementationContext.context: This implementation restricts AWS Lambda API calls against your function with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key, while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`). Requests that do not satisfy that condition are denied, so unauthenticated callers cannot invoke your function or read its configuration.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. For anonymous requests, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` and `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths` are not included in the request context and `aws:PrincipalAccount` is set to `anonymous`. Requiring these keys to match your organization or account values therefore helps prevent unauthenticated access. For requests by AWS service principals, these keys do not contain your organization or account values, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation validates the granted action (`$.Action`), the grantee (`$.Principal`), and the function URL auth type condition (`$.FunctionUrlAuthType`) that a permission statement declares. Stack operations that grant `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` publicly under the `NONE` auth type are denied, so unauthenticated callers are restricted from invoking your function.

This implementation evaluates the `$.PolicyDocument` you declare for your function's resource-based policy and identifies documents that can grant public access. Stack operations declaring such a document are denied, so unauthenticated callers are restricted from invoking your function.

This implementation evaluates the declared policy document with the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy check `CheckNoPublicAccess`. This check uses automated reasoning to evaluate whether a resource-based policy can grant public access.

links.title: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks

implementationContext.context: This implementation checks the function URL auth type declared in `$.AuthType`, requiring `AWS_IAM` rather than `NONE` when the URL is created or updated. Rejecting a URL that declares `NONE` helps address the mitigation by preventing deployment of an endpoint that skips IAM authentication.

This rule checks the function URL auth type recorded at `$.FunctionUrlConfigs[*].AuthType`, flagging any URL that reports `NONE` rather than `AWS_IAM`. It also submits your function's resource-based policy to a public-access check, where `$.result` reports whether that policy can grant unauthenticated invocation.

This Config rule evaluates your function's resource-based policy by calling the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy check `CheckNoPublicAccess`. That check uses automated reasoning to report whether the policy can grant public access to your function.

links.title: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks

guidance.description: Consider using AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer external access analyzers to review your functions and layer versions. These analyzers help identify resources in your accounts that are shared with identities outside your zone of trust. An external access analyzer evaluates the resource-based policies attached to your functions and layer versions. It generates a finding for each policy that grants access to a principal outside your zone of trust. Each finding names the resource, the identity that was granted access, and the permissions granted. Review each finding to determine whether the access is intended. If necessary, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice. External access findings cover only resources in the Region where the analyzer is enabled. Create an analyzer in each Region where you run functions or publish layer versions. External access is not reported for resource-based policies attached to aliases or to specific versions invoked through a qualified ARN.

links.title: Using AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer

implementationContext.context: This recommendation directs you to review the resource-based policies on your functions for access granted to identities outside your organization. Remediating any unintended grants helps you keep access to your functions limited to trusted identities.

This implementation restricts AWS Lambda API calls against your function with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` and `aws:SourceOrgID` condition keys, while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`). Requests that do not satisfy those conditions are denied, so identities outside your organization cannot invoke or modify the function.

Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities and to services acting on your behalf.

As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`.

To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys.

Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation checks `$.Principal`, `$.PrincipalOrgID`, `$.SourceAccount`, and `$.SourceArn` on the function resource-based policy statement a template declares. A statement naming an account, organization, or source that you do not permit is rejected before the permission is created.

A hook on this resource type can reject a permission statement before it is added to your function's policy. Validate `$.Principal` so that a template cannot grant access to identities outside your organization. Validate `$.PrincipalOrgID` so that an organization-wide grant names only your own organization.

This implementation recommends using both Access Analyzer basic policy checks and custom policy checks. Basic policy checks (`ValidatePolicy`) validate your policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices. These checks do not use automated reasoning, but do provide actionable recommendations that help you author policies that are functional and conform to security best practices. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance, provably verifying that a policy does not grant public access, grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain, or grant specified permissions. The reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource; the check fails when the resource policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

links.title: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples

implementationContext.context: This implementation validates `$.PolicyDocument`, the resource-based policy on your function, before CloudFormation attaches it. Rejecting grants that reach beyond the principals you allowlist helps limit function access to trusted identities.

A CloudFormation template can grant access to your function through principal and organization-identifier properties on Lambda permission resources. Values naming identities outside your organization may grant unintended cross-account access. Validating `$.PolicyDocument` at deployment time helps you review those grants before the policy is attached.

This implementation recommends using both IAM Access Analyzer basic policy checks and custom policy checks.

Basic policy checks validate your policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices by calling `ValidatePolicy`. These checks do not use automated reasoning. They do provide actionable recommendations that help you author functional policies that conform to security best practices.

Custom policy checks use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. Calling `CheckNoPublicAccess` verifies that a policy does not grant public access. Calling `CheckNoNewAccess` verifies that it does not grant access beyond a reference policy you maintain. Calling `CheckAccessNotGranted` verifies that it does not grant permissions you specify.

The reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to your function. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples

implementationContext.context: This implementation captures each `AddPermission` and `AddLayerVersionPermission` call in CloudTrail along with the requested `$.Principal`, `$.PrincipalOrgID`, `$.SourceArn`, `$.SourceAccount`, and `$.OrganizationId` values. Reviewing those grants helps you detect resource-based policy statements that extend function or layer access beyond trusted principals.

Both `AddPermission` and `AddLayerVersionPermission` write statements into a resource-based policy that grants other identities access to your function or layer version. Monitoring these calls surfaces the principal and organization scoping that each request carries. Each event also records the identity that made the call. If necessary, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

This implementation inspects the function's resource-based policy recorded at `$.supplementaryConfiguration.Policy` for public access grants and for statements missing the `aws:SourceArn` or `aws:SourceAccount` condition keys. Flagging those policies helps you detect invoke access that is not limited to trusted identities.

This implementation recommends using both Access Analyzer basic policy checks and custom policy checks.

Basic policy checks (ValidatePolicy) validate your policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices. These checks do not use automated reasoning, but do provide actionable recommendations that help you author policies that are functional and conform to security best practices.

Custom policy checks (CheckNoPublicAccess, CheckNoNewAccess, CheckAccessNotGranted) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance, provably verifying that a policy does not grant public access, grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain, or grant specified permissions.

The reference policy for CheckNoNewAccess allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource; the check fails when the resource policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

External access findings, generated by an external access analyzer, also use automated reasoning to identify resource policies that allow access from outside your zone of trust.

implementationContext.context: This implementation governs `lambda:InvokeFunction` and `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` on your function with the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceOrgID` condition keys. As a result, AWS services acting on your behalf are restricted from invoking your function on behalf of resources outside your organization.

To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

This implementation checks a function permission at create time, requiring `$.SourceArn` or `$.SourceAccount` when `$.Principal` names an AWS service. Without one of those source values, other accounts could configure their own resources to invoke your function.

This implementation validates `$.PolicyDocument`, the resource-based policy on your Lambda resource, at create time. It prevents grants to an AWS service principal that omit `aws:SourceArn` or `aws:SourceAccount`, scoping cross-service access to the resources and accounts you name.

This implementation uses IAM Access Analyzer basic policy checks. These checks validate a policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices. They do not use automated reasoning. The hook calls `ValidatePolicy` with the policy document from your template. It then inspects the findings for a security warning that a statement grants an AWS service principal access without a source condition. Adding `aws:SourceArn` or `aws:SourceAccount` resolves that warning.

This rule submits the function's recorded resource policy at `$.supplementaryConfiguration.Policy` to a policy validation check for missing source conditions. Flagging grants that omit `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` helps you find functions a service could be induced to invoke for an untrusted resource.

This implementation recommends using Access Analyzer basic policy checks.

Basic policy checks (ValidatePolicy) validate your policy against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices. These checks do not use automated reasoning, but do provide actionable recommendations that help you author policies that are functional and conform to security best practices.

CloudTrail records `AddPermission`, `PutResourcePolicy`, and `RemovePermission` calls that rewrite your function's resource-based policy. Flagging changes to `$.Action` and `$.Policy` helps you detect attempts to broaden which principals can request the deployment package presigned URL.

CloudTrail records each `GetFunction` call, which returns the Amazon S3 presigned URL for downloading a function's deployment package. Recording `$.FunctionName` with the caller's identity and network origin helps you review whether only selected principals requested that package. If a call is unexpected, you can follow up with the responsive controls of your choice.

This implementation restricts `lambda:GetFunction` with the `aws:PrincipalTag/<key>` condition key, limiting the action to select principals. Requests from other principals are denied, so they cannot obtain the Amazon S3 presigned URL used to download the function's deployment package.

The download link that `GetFunction` returns is an Amazon S3 presigned URL that AWS Lambda signs with its own service principal. Conditions that evaluate the calling principal's request context do not apply once that URL is issued. Restricting `lambda:GetFunction` to select principals is therefore the preventive lever available to you. Principals that need only the function's settings can call `GetFunctionConfiguration` instead.

links.title: Data perimeter example SCP: restrict service-principal presigned URLs

implementationContext.context: To restrict access to select principals, use the `aws:PrincipalArn` or `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` condition keys. Use `aws:PrincipalArn` to specify the Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) of the principals. Those ARNs can follow a naming convention or an IAM path that scopes the restriction to a set of principals without enumerating each one. Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to identify those principals by a tag attached to them. Choose the condition key that matches your IAM policy management strategy.

This implementation validates owner and purpose metadata in `$.Tags[*].Key` and `$.Tags[*].Value` before the function is created. Functions missing those tags are not deployed, helping keep each function traceable to an accountable owner and business purpose.

This rule flags a Lambda function when the tag keys recorded at `$.tags[*].key` omit the owner and purpose keys you require. Attributing each function to an accountable owner and a business purpose helps you triage findings and route them to the right team.

This implementation restricts `lambda:CreateFunction` and `lambda:TagResource` on your functions with the `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, and `aws:TagKeys` condition keys. Requests that do not satisfy these conditions are denied, which helps each function you create or tag receive owner and purpose tags. This implementation also restricts `lambda:UntagResource` with the `aws:TagKeys` condition key, so requests that remove the owner or purpose tag key are denied.

Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

This hook requires the Lambda Insights extension layer in `$.Layers[*]` and the `AWS_LAMBDA_EXEC_WRAPPER` key in `$.Environment.Variables{key}`. Deployments that omit either setting are denied, so your functions collect detailed CloudWatch metrics.

This implementation records `CreateFunction` and `UpdateFunctionConfiguration` calls, including the `$.Layers[*]` value that lists the layers attached to your function. Reviewing these events helps address the mitigation by showing when the layers that carry Lambda Insights and Application Signals were set.

This detective rule checks `$.configuration.layers[*].arn` for the Lambda Insights and CloudWatch Application Signals layers, plus the `AWS_LAMBDA_EXEC_WRAPPER` entry in `$.Environment.Variables{key}`. It identifies functions that collect only the default CloudWatch metrics rather than the detailed metrics these settings enable.

guidance.description:
Configure the security groups named in your function's VPC configuration following least-privilege best practices. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the sources, destinations, protocols, and ports your function requires. Sources and destinations can be IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any IP address, such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Pay particular attention to outbound rules, because a VPC-attached function's traffic is predominantly egress.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope each policy by account, organizational unit, or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group to the resources in scope. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow-list or a block-list. It flags non-compliant security groups in a central dashboard, notifies you, and can automatically remediate them. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Then run an analysis with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope` and `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

links.title: Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager
How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager

implementationContext.context: This recommendation directs you to restrict the inbound and outbound rules on your function's VPC security groups to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Traffic to or from any other address, protocol, or port is then not permitted by those groups.

This implementation validates the groups named in `$.VpcConfig.SecurityGroupIds[*]` at deploy time, resolving `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions` and `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress`. Functions that would attach groups permitting unrestricted inbound or outbound traffic are not created, helping reduce your function's network exposure.

This implementation resolves the security groups recorded at `$.Functions[*].VpcConfig.SecurityGroupIds[*]` and inspects their inbound and outbound rules. Flagging rules that admit `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` on sensitive ports or all protocols helps you detect functions with broader network exposure than they need.

This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition key in a service control policy (SCP) to govern `lambda:GetLayerVersion`, `lambda:GetLayerVersionPolicy`, `lambda:PublishLayerVersion`, `lambda:DeleteLayerVersion`, `lambda:AddLayerVersionPermission`, and `lambda:RemoveLayerVersionPermission`. This condition helps prevent access to layers outside your organization; it takes effect at the `GetLayerVersion` request that issues a layer archive's 10-minute download link, not at the download itself.

AWS services such as Amazon CloudWatch and AWS AppConfig publish Lambda extensions as layers that your functions can add. Those layers are hosted in AWS-owned accounts outside your organization. Exclude their layer ARNs from this statement so your identities can keep using them. The default resource perimeter policy example shows this exclusion. The service-owned resources reference lists the ARN patterns to exclude.

To restrict access to trusted resources, use the `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`, or `aws:ResourceAccount` condition keys. These scope access to resources that belong to a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

At create time, this implementation validates `$.Principal`, the account granted layer usage permission, and `$.OrganizationId`, the organization that scopes a wildcard principal. Stack operations granting `lambda:GetLayerVersion` to accounts outside your organization are blocked, which helps limit who can download your layer archives.

This implementation validates `$.Principal` and `$.OrganizationId` at create time, rejecting a layer version permission that grants `lambda:GetLayerVersion` to all AWS accounts. Requiring a named account or an organization scope helps limit which principals can read your layer archive.

Layer version permissions are declared in CloudFormation as `AWS::Lambda::LayerVersionPermission` resources. A hook on this resource type can reject a template whose `$.Principal` names an account outside your organization. It can also require `$.OrganizationId` to name your own organization whenever `$.Principal` is set to the wildcard value. This helps keep an unscoped wildcard grant from reaching your layer versions through a stack deployment.

This implementation inspects each layer version's resource-based policy at `$.Policy` and flags wildcard-principal grants of `lambda:GetLayerVersion` that carry no `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition. Flagging those grants helps you detect layer versions readable by every AWS account rather than a defined set of principals.

guidance.description: Consider using AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer external access analyzers to help identify layer versions in your accounts that are shared with untrusted identities. Also use these external access analyzers to help identify functions in your accounts that are shared with untrusted identities. Layer version permissions can grant `lambda:GetLayerVersion` outside your account. That read access returns a link to download the layer archive. Review each finding to confirm whether the sharing is intended. If necessary, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

links.title: AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer

implementationContext.context: This recommendation directs you to identify layer versions whose resource-based policy shares `lambda:GetLayerVersion` with identities outside your organization. Remediating unintended sharing helps keep your layer content accessible only to trusted identities, including AWS services acting on your behalf.

This implementation records `AddLayerVersionPermission` calls, capturing the grant recipient in the `$.Principal` request parameter and the organization scope in `$.OrganizationId`. Reviewing these events helps you detect a layer version policy change that shares your layer with identities outside your organization.

A layer version policy can grant layer usage to a single account, to all accounts in an organization, or to all AWS accounts. The `$.Principal` request parameter records the recipient of that grant. The `$.OrganizationId` request parameter records the organization it is scoped to. Reviewing both parameters helps you identify a layer version shared with identities outside your organization. You can then remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

This rule reads each layer version's resource-based policy at `$.Policy` and identifies grants of `lambda:GetLayerVersion` to other accounts or to all accounts. Reporting those grants helps you keep layer content readable only by trusted identities.

Your AWS Config rule evaluates each layer version's resource-based policy with IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks use automated reasoning to analyze the policy document.

`CheckNoNewAccess` compares that policy against a reference policy you maintain. Your reference policy allowlists the principals that may be granted access. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

`CheckAccessNotGranted` checks whether that policy grants the actions you list.

An external access analyzer reports resource-based policies that allow access from outside your organization. Your rule reads those findings with `ListFindingsV2`.

links.title: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks
IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples

implementationContext.context: This implementation restricts `lambda:AddLayerVersionPermission` and `lambda:AddPermission`, while exempting principals tagged for exclusion from the identity perimeter with the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:identity` condition key. Requests from other principals are denied, so they cannot grant other accounts access to your layer versions.

AWS Lambda is not among the services that support resource control policies (RCPs). A service control policy (SCP) is therefore the preventive guardrail available for its resource-based policies. `lambda:AddLayerVersionPermission` and `lambda:AddPermission` can grant other accounts or AWS services access to a layer version or a function. Restricting these actions to select principals helps prevent grants to identities outside your organization.
